items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: one day Philly Joe Billy Joe grabbed me one day and said, 'Man, come over here to the Blue Note, and make this date with Lee Morlin and Horace Silver and Billy and myself'

ctx.x: And Wilbur Campbell went back to Chicago, and Frankie Dunlap made one side of the record, too, because Wilbur had to leave the next month after the initial side, and Junior Mance had left, and so we used Kenny Drew down at Birdland, but it was a beautiful night, and amost every other night, I had ... Monday night I had a job down there.

And he called me up for a gig -- Mr. Stan Getz, and Elvin Jones, Wynton Elmer, Joe Kelly and myself, and we were working -- that's Red Garland, Philly Joe, Trane, Paul, and himself opposite the Miles Davis Quintet -- at Birdland.

Naturally, we were gonna cook -- we were gonna play our best, too, and not realizing, you know, Stan Getz -- he's a star; naturally he's a star, but we want to get behind and push him just as much; the rhythm section was pushing Miles. And I don't know, Stan was going through his little problems during that time, and the other one was playing all those poly-rhythms, and Stan was getting confused; he didn't know what to do, so after the first set, we come off the bandstand, and he says, "Elvin" and Elton turned…

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: Philly Billy Joe and Kenny Drew was the rhythm section... Drew, myself, Philly filled in most of the time

ctx.x: Philly Billy Joe and Kenny Drew was the rhythm section; we didn't know it at that moment, because

they had -- let's see who else came in? Drew, myself, Philly filled in most of the time; yeah, A.T. a couple of times. But we did an album with Ernie Louie Henry called 'Presenting Ernie Louie Henry' -- Arthur Taylor, Kenny Dorham, [Jim Knight], or whatever. But we made that, and oh, started recording with Dick Stig Johnson, this altoist, Dave McKenna, a pianist, and Billy Joe, and who else? Oh, my goodness, I started recording with everybody they would bring in there.

I'd be downstairs, in the garage, you know, sleeping and he'd say, 'Keepnews All right Wilbur, you got a record date tomorrow -- where's your fiddle?' Now, as long as I'm working, my fiddle was around, you know, but when the office pawn it and is closed, like on a - say, if I'm not working, I'd get it out Monday morning, you know, and that was the fiddle that Oscar Pettiford gave me now, when he saw me in New York.
